name: Worst case
intent: Write a dreaded outcome out concretely, so it stops weighing more than it would.
when: a fear too large to think about clearly, not tied to one plan (for a plan's failure, use pre-mortem)
prompt: Name it plainly. Then write what would actually happen, and what you would do.
readback: Compare the before and after weights. If the day/week/month boxes stay abstract ('everything would fall apart'), the exercise didn't land. Ask for the concrete next step instead.

claims.claim: Writing out a dreaded outcome concretely, including what would happen next and how one would cope, lowers its felt severity. People overestimate how bad and how long-lasting their reaction to negative events will be.
claims.construct: decatastrophising (cognitive therapy); the impact bias and immune neglect in affective forecasting

claims.claim: People recall their earlier attitudes, feelings or confidence as closer to their present state than they were, or as fitting their theory of how they must have changed. A written baseline is therefore needed to see real change.
claims.construct: consistency and change biases in autobiographical memory (implicit theories of stability and change)

grounding.helps: when a dread belongs to no plan: people overestimate how long a bad outcome will hurt, and in forecasting studies thinking about everything else that will fill the following days reduced that overestimate; the before and after ratings show whether the page did the same for you
grounding.backfires: when the next-day, week and month block only rehearses the catastrophe, without the other things that will fill those days, which may feed worry (untested), or when defusing the dread makes a real risk feel acceptable
